analogy.p: Imagine a long corridor. Near the top (the upper course) a few strong, energetic pupils squeeze through a narrow space and push straight down the stairs, which is vertical erosion. As more pupils join (tributaries), the corridor gets wider and the crowd takes bends: on the outside of each corner pupils crash into the wall and wear it away (erosion), while on the inside they slow down and pile up (deposition). Right at the end, at the canteen doors (the mouth), the crowd slows and spreads out, dropping their bags everywhere like silt in an estuary. The analogy breaks down because pupils choose their own route, whereas a river's path is controlled only by gravity, rock type and the energy of the water.
analogy.t: A river is a school corridor at break time

bullets: Know the **long profile** (a line from source to mouth showing height against distance) and the **cross profile** (a slice across the channel and valley).
Know how **channel characteristics** change downstream: width, depth, velocity, discharge, load size and shape, and gradient.
Know four processes of **erosion**, four of **transportation** and the reasons for **deposition**.
Be able to explain, in labelled stages, how each named landform forms.
Be able to link the landforms to the course of the river: upper, middle and lower.
Use a **UK river valley** (for example the River Tees) as a named example, with specific places, but check this against the example your teacher taught.
Command words: **describe** (say what), **explain** (give reasons and linked steps), **annotate**, **suggest**.
**Link to other topics:** flood risk and management (levees, floodplains, hydrographs) and coasts (erosion and deposition processes are very similar).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: For rivers, AQA expects you to describe and explain the **long profile** and **cross profile** of a river and its valley, and how the channel changes from source to mouth. You must understand the **fluvial processes** of erosion (hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition, solution), transportation (traction, saltation, suspension, solution) and deposition, and then use them to explain how distinctive landforms form. The landforms are grouped by the process that dominates: erosional (interlocking spurs, waterfalls and gorges), erosional and depositional together (meanders and oxbow lakes) and depositional (levees, floodplains and estuaries). Almost every exam question on this topic is really asking 'which process is acting, where, and why', so learn the processes first and the landforms become step-by-step applications of them.

bullets: **Source:** where the river begins, often a spring or a small stream high in the hills.
**Mouth:** where the river meets the sea (or a lake); in the UK this is usually an estuary.
**Tributary:** a smaller stream or river that flows into a larger river.
**Confluence:** the point where two rivers or streams meet.
**Watershed:** the boundary of high land separating one drainage basin from another.
**Channel:** the path the water flows along, with a bed (floor) and banks (sides).
**Load:** all the material (rock, sediment, dissolved minerals) that the river carries.
**Discharge:** the volume of water passing a point each second, measured in cubic metres per second (cumecs).
core.h: The language of a river system
core.p: A river flows within a **drainage basin**, the area of land drained by a river and its tributaries. The edge of the basin is the **watershed**, a ridge of high land; rain falling on one side drains into this river and rain falling on the other side drains into a different one. The river starts at its **source**, usually in highland, is joined by **tributaries** at **confluences**, and ends at its **mouth** where it enters a sea or lake. Using these words precisely wins marks and stops you losing them in descriptions.

bullets: Upper course: **steep gradient**, high potential energy, dominated by **vertical erosion** and the transport of large angular load.
Middle course: **gentler gradient**, more discharge, dominated by **lateral erosion** (sideways) and transport.
Lower course: **very gentle gradient**, the river is near **base level**, dominated by **deposition**.
Real long profiles are not perfectly smooth: waterfalls, rapids and lakes break the curve.
Gradient falls downstream but the river still flows fast: it is the **efficient, deep, smooth channel** (not the steepness) that gives high velocity.
Exam tip: when describing a long profile graph, quote heights and distances (for example 'falls from 600 m to 50 m in the first 20 km').
**Higher tier idea:** the river is trying to reach a balance between erosion and deposition called a **graded profile**, but it never fully succeeds because discharge and rock type keep changing.
**Link to other topics:** the shape of the long profile controls where erosion and deposition happen, and therefore where landforms form.
core.h: The long profile: why it is a concave curve
core.p: The long profile of a river is the gradient of the river from its source to its mouth. It is a **concave** curve: steep in the upper course, gentler in the middle course and almost flat in the lower course. Upstream the river has a great deal of potential energy because it is high above sea level, and it uses that energy for **vertical erosion**, cutting downwards into the bed. As the river nears its mouth it can only cut down as far as **base level** (usually sea level), so its energy is used for lateral erosion and transport and the gradient flattens. Over very long periods erosion upstream and deposition downstream smooth the profile into this curve.

bullets: Upper course: **V-shaped valley**, steep sides, narrow shallow channel, interlocking spurs.
Middle course: valley sides **less steep** and valley floor wider, with a wider, deeper channel and meanders beginning.
Lower course: **wide, flat valley floor** (floodplain), very wide and deep channel, levees and sometimes an estuary.
Channel **width** and **depth** both increase downstream because **discharge** increases as tributaries join and groundwater adds more water.
**Velocity** usually increases downstream: the bed is smoother and the channel is deeper and more efficient (less friction with the bed and banks) even though the gradient is gentler.
Load gets **smaller and more rounded** downstream because of **attrition** (pieces knocking together and wearing down) and sorting.
Upstream the load is large, **angular** boulders; downstream it is fine silt and clay.
Exam tip: always give **direction** (increases or decreases downstream) and a **reason** with an 'because'.
core.h: The cross profile and valley shape change downstream
core.p: A cross profile shows the shape of the channel and valley when you slice across them. In the upper course the valley is **narrow and V-shaped** with steep sides, because the river erodes **downwards** and weathering and mass movement supply loose material from the slopes. In the middle course the valley widens as **lateral erosion** begins to cut into the banks, and in the lower course the valley is wide and flat with a broad **floodplain** either side of a wide, deep channel. Remember that the valley shape and the channel shape are related but not identical, so say which one you are describing.

bullets: **Width:** narrow upstream, wide downstream, because more water and lateral erosion.
**Depth:** shallow upstream, deeper downstream, because discharge increases.
**Velocity:** lower upstream (rough bed, large boulders, shallow water cause friction), higher downstream (smooth bed, efficient channel).
**Discharge:** low upstream, high downstream, as tributaries and groundwater add water.
**Load size:** large and angular upstream, small and rounded downstream (attrition).
**Gradient:** steep upstream, gentle downstream.
Formula: **discharge (m3/s) = cross-sectional area (m2) x velocity (m/s)**, where area = width x average depth.
A river can have fast flow in the upper course during a flood or over a steep waterfall, so use 'generally' or 'usually' in written answers.
core.h: Channel changes downstream: a quick comparison
core.p: Examiners love a table or data question on channel characteristics, so you should be able to describe each of the six variables and give the reason. Discharge is calculated as cross-sectional area times velocity, where the area is width times average depth, which is why a wider, deeper channel carries far more water even if the velocity only rises a little. Because all of these variables are linked, a change in one explains the change in another, and the strongest answers say so.

bullets: **Hydraulic action:** force of water compresses air in cracks, weakening and removing rock.
**Abrasion:** load scrapes and grinds the bed and banks; makes the channel deeper and wider.
**Attrition:** load collides and wears itself down; **rocks become smaller and rounder**, it does not erode the channel.
**Solution:** chemical process where soluble minerals (for example in limestone and chalk) dissolve in the water.
**Vertical erosion** dominates in the upper course, giving V-shaped valleys and waterfalls.
**Lateral erosion** dominates in the middle and lower courses, widening the valley and forming meanders.
Erosion is fastest when **velocity and discharge are high** (floods), when the load is large and angular, and when the rock is soft or heavily jointed.
Common mark-scheme phrase: 'abrasion is where the river's load wears away the bed and banks'.
core.p: Erosion is the wearing away and removal of rock, and in a river it happens in four ways. **Hydraulic action** is the sheer force of the water: it pushes air into cracks in the bed and banks, the air is compressed, and the pressure weakens and breaks off pieces of rock. **Abrasion** is when the river's load (rocks and pebbles) is thrown against and scrapes the bed and banks like sandpaper, which is the most effective erosion process in a river. **Attrition** is when pieces of load knock against each other and break into smaller, rounder, smoother pieces, and **solution** (corrosion) is when soluble rocks like limestone are dissolved by slightly acidic water. Note the difference: abrasion wears away the channel, whereas attrition wears away the load itself.

bullets: **Traction:** large boulders and rocks are rolled or dragged along the river bed.
**Saltation:** pebbles and small stones are lifted by the flow, move a short distance and bounce back down, over and over.
**Suspension:** very small particles such as silt and clay are carried along within the water, which makes the river look muddy.
**Solution:** dissolved minerals (for example calcium carbonate) are carried invisibly in the water.
Larger particles need **faster, higher-energy flow**: the biggest load moves only during floods.
Most of a river's load is carried near the bed in the upper course and in suspension and solution in the lower course.
Exam tip: link each process to a **particle size** (boulder, pebble, silt/clay, dissolved) to earn the second mark.
**Link to other topics:** coastal transportation uses the same four words plus longshore drift.
core.p: Transportation is the movement of eroded material by the river, and the method depends on the size of the particle and the energy (velocity and discharge) of the river. The largest boulders are pushed along the bed by **traction**, pebbles and gravel bounce along by **saltation**, fine silt and clay are carried within the water by **suspension**, and dissolved minerals are carried invisibly in **solution**. When the river floods, velocity and discharge rocket, so it can carry far larger material than normal, which is why floods change channels so quickly. The river's **capacity** is the total load it can carry and its **competence** is the biggest particle it can move, and both rise when velocity rises.

bullets: Deposition occurs when **velocity decreases** and the river loses energy.

Reasons for deposition: shallow water, inside of meander bends, river entering the sea or a lake, **reduced discharge** (drought), flood waters spreading across the floodplain, more load than the river can carry.
Coarsest material is deposited **first**; fine silt and clay are carried furthest.
Depositional landforms: **levees, floodplains, estuary mudflats**, and slip-off slopes inside meanders.
Alluvium is **fertile**, so floodplains are good farmland and attractive for settlement.
In the lower course there is more deposition than erosion because the gradient is gentle and the river is near base level.
Exam tip: always state the **cause** (energy is lost because ...) before the effect (so the load is dropped).
**Link to other topics:** the same logic explains beaches, spits and bars on the coast.
core.h: Deposition: when and why a river drops its load
core.p: Deposition happens when a river **loses energy** and can no longer carry its load. This occurs when the velocity falls, for example on the inside of a meander bend, where the water is shallow and slow, or when the river enters the sea or a lake and its water slows right down. It also occurs when discharge falls (in a dry period), when the river floods and spreads across the floodplain so it becomes shallower and slower, and when there is a large amount of load to carry. Material is deposited in order of size: the **heaviest, largest** pieces first and the finest silt and clay last, which is called sorting. Deposited river sediment is called **alluvium**.

bullets: Found in the **upper course** where the valley is a steep V-shape.
The river has **low discharge but high potential energy**, so vertical erosion dominates.
The river is too small to erode laterally, so it **bends around** the harder ridges of land.
The spurs from one side **overlap or interlock** with those from the other side when seen from above.
Weathering and mass movement on the valley sides add load and steepen the V-shape.
A 4-mark answer needs: upper course, vertical erosion, river winds around resistant land, spurs interlock.
Sketch tip: draw the river as a thin wavy line zig-zagging between alternating ridges.
**Link to other topics:** the same upland climate and rocks give waterfalls and gorges in the same part of the river.
core.p: Interlocking spurs are **ridges of high land that stick out from alternate sides** of a V-shaped valley and appear to fit together like the teeth of a zip. In the upper course the river has lots of energy but little discharge, so it cannot erode sideways and cut through the ridges. Instead it erodes **vertically**, cutting a deep narrow valley and winding around the more resistant ridges, leaving the spurs sticking out. The sides of the valley are also broken down by weathering and moved down the slope by mass movement, which creates the steep V-shape.

bullets: Step 1: river flows over a band of **hard rock** lying over **soft rock**.
Step 2: soft rock erodes faster by **hydraulic action** and **abrasion**, creating a step.
Step 3: a **plunge pool** forms at the base because of the force of falling water and swirling rocks (abrasion).
Step 4: hard rock is **undercut**, leaving an **overhang**.
Step 5: overhang becomes unsupported and **collapses**; the waterfall **retreats upstream**.
Step 6: repeated retreat leaves a deep, steep-sided **gorge** downstream of the waterfall.
Always state the difference in resistance: it is **differential erosion** that makes the waterfall.
Example: **High Force, River Tees** (hard Whin Sill dolerite over softer sedimentary rocks); check you can name your own example.
core.p: A waterfall forms where a river flows over a band of **hard (resistant) rock** that lies above a band of **softer (less resistant) rock**. The soft rock is eroded faster by hydraulic action and abrasion, which undercuts the hard rock and leaves an overhang. Water plunging over the edge swirls at the base and erodes a deep **plunge pool** which deepens the undercut. Eventually the unsupported overhang becomes too heavy and **collapses**, and the fallen rocks are swirled around the plunge pool, causing further abrasion. Repeated over thousands of years the waterfall **retreats upstream** and leaves a steep-sided, narrow valley called a **gorge**. An example is High Force on the River Tees, where hard igneous rock lies over softer sedimentary rock.

bullets: Found in the **middle and lower courses**, where **lateral erosion** is important.
**Outside bend:** water flows faster and deeper, so more **erosion** by hydraulic action and abrasion, forming a **river cliff**.
**Inside bend:** water is slower and shallower, so **deposition** occurs, forming a **slip-off slope**.
**Helicoidal flow** (spiral flow) moves material from the outer bank towards the inner bank.
The cross-section of a meander is **asymmetrical**: steep and deep on the outside, gently sloping and shallow on the inside.
Meanders migrate **downstream** over time, widening the floodplain.
Mark-scheme words: 'erosion on the outside bend creates a river cliff; deposition on the inside bend creates a slip-off slope'.
**Link to other topics:** meanders lead to oxbow lakes and widen the floodplain.
core.p: A meander is a **large bend in a river** that forms in the middle and lower courses where the river has a gentle gradient and lots of discharge. Water flows fastest on the **outside** of the bend where the channel is deeper, so there is more erosion, forming a steep **river cliff**. On the **inside** of the bend the water is slow and shallow, so the river deposits sediment and builds a gently sloping **slip-off slope** (a small beach of sand and shingle). A corkscrew-shaped flow called helicoidal flow carries eroded material from the outside bank across the channel and drops it on the inside. Over time the bends get bigger and move downstream as the outside erodes and the inside builds out.

bullets: Step 1: **erosion** of the outside bends makes the meanders bigger and the **neck** narrower.
Step 2: during a **flood** the river breaks through the neck and takes the shorter route.
Step 3: the river now flows through the **new straight channel** at higher speed.
Step 4: **deposition** seals the ends of the old meander with alluvium, because the water slows at the edges.
Step 5: the old meander is cut off and becomes an **oxbow lake**.
Step 6: with time the lake can dry out and become a **meander scar** (marshy hollow).
A 6-mark answer needs the **sequence**, with erosion, flood and deposition each named.
Common confusion: oxbow lakes need both **erosion and deposition**, not deposition alone.
core.p: An oxbow lake is a **crescent-shaped lake** found on a floodplain beside a river, and it forms from a meander that gets cut off. As erosion continues on the outside bends of a meander, the neck of land between two bends becomes narrower. Eventually, usually during a **flood**, when the river has a lot of energy, the river breaks through the neck and takes the shorter, straighter route. Deposition then seals off the ends of the old loop using alluvium, because the water slows down at the edges of the new channel, and the abandoned meander becomes a lake. Over time the lake dries up, leaving a **meander scar**.

bullets: **Floodplain:** wide, flat, **fertile** land; formed by **lateral erosion** (meander migration) and **deposition** during floods.
Floodplains give **good farmland**, flat building land and easy transport, but are at risk of **flooding**.
**Levees:** natural raised embankments next to the channel built by repeated floods.
Flood water loses energy when it leaves the channel, so the **coarse material is dropped first** next to the river.
Over time the river can flow **above** the level of the floodplain, which increases the risk when levees fail.
Artificial levees (**embankments**) are a form of **hard engineering** used to protect towns.
Exam tip: 'levees form because heavier sediment is dropped first when the river floods and loses energy'.
**Link to other topics:** flood risk and management (flood plain zoning, hard engineering with embankments).
core.p: A floodplain is the **wide, flat area of land either side of a river** that is covered with water when the river floods. It is formed by two processes working together: lateral erosion and meander migration widen the valley floor, and repeated floods **deposit layers of alluvium** (silt and clay) that build it up. Levees are **natural raised banks** along the sides of the river channel. When a river floods, the water spills out of the channel and loses energy and velocity as it spreads, so the **coarsest, heaviest material is deposited first, right next to the channel**, while finer silt is carried further out onto the floodplain. After many floods the deposits build into ridges that raise the banks, so the channel can hold more water.

bullets: Estuary = **tidal mouth** of a river, where the river meets the sea.
Very wide, with large areas of **mudflats** exposed at low tide.
Formed by **deposition** of fine silt and clay as the river slows and meets the tide.
Salt water makes clay particles **clump together and settle** (flocculation).
Home to rich wildlife (wading birds feed on mudflats) and often protected sites.
Useful for **ports and industry** because of deep channels and sheltered water.
Salt marshes absorb wave energy and can reduce flood risk.
**Link to other topics:** coastal landforms and management; sea level rise threatens estuary towns.
core.p: An estuary is the **wide, tidal mouth of a river** where fresh river water meets salt water from the sea. The water flows in and out with the tide twice a day, which makes the estuary a place of constant mixing. The river is slow and wide here, so **fine silt and clay are deposited** as **mudflats**, and salt marsh develops on higher ground. Salt in sea water causes fine clay particles to clump together (flocculation) and sink, which speeds up deposition. Meanwhile, the tides scour a deep central channel, which is why ships and ports use estuaries. UK examples include the Humber and Severn estuaries.

bullets: **Upper course:** V-shaped valley, interlocking spurs, waterfalls, gorges, rapids; vertical erosion, large angular load.
**Middle course:** meanders, river cliffs, slip-off slopes, wider channel; lateral erosion and transport.
**Lower course:** floodplain, levees, oxbow lakes, estuary; deposition, small rounded load.
Energy and load change together: steep and rough upstream, gentle and smooth downstream.
Land use follows landforms: upland farming and reservoirs upstream; towns and farmland on flat, fertile floodplains; ports at estuaries.
Challenges: **flooding** on floodplains, steep slopes and difficult access upstream.
Good answers refer to **named places** from the case study, not just general features.
**Link to other topics:** use this chain when answering flood-risk and hydrograph questions.
core.h: Putting it together: a river valley from source to mouth
core.p: A good student can walk down a river in their head and name what happens. Near the **source** the river is small and steep and cuts vertically, forming a V-shaped valley with interlocking spurs and perhaps a waterfall and gorge. In the **middle course** the river widens and starts lateral erosion, forming meanders with river cliffs and slip-off slopes, and may cut off a loop to make an oxbow lake. In the **lower course** the river is wide and slow, with a floodplain and levees, and finally it reaches the sea in an estuary with mudflats. On the River Tees, for example, the upper valley has High Force waterfall in a gorge, the middle course has meanders and the lower course reaches the Teesmouth estuary, but check this against your own named example.

exam: **Describe** = say what you see; use data and direction ('width increases from 2 m to 15 m'). Do not explain unless asked.
**Explain** = give a reason using 'because' or 'so'; most 4-mark landform questions are one mark per linked step.
**Explain the formation of a landform (4 marks):** name the process, say where it acts, give two or three steps in order, and name the final landform.
**6-mark formation answers (for example oxbow lake):** write a numbered sequence with at least three separate named processes and a clear start-to-finish chain.
Use **exact process names**: hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition, solution; traction, saltation, suspension, solution.
Always state the **rock type difference** (hard/resistant over soft/less resistant) when explaining waterfalls.
Link **location to process**: 'in the upper course, vertical erosion dominates because the river has high potential energy'.
On **long profile and cross profile graphs**, quote heights, distances and widths with units, and describe the shape (concave, V-shaped, wide and flat).
Draw **labelled sketch diagrams** if allowed: label river cliff, slip-off slope, plunge pool, overhang and neck; sketches can earn marks.
For **named example** questions, include at least two place names and one fact (for example High Force on the River Tees).

mistakes.r: Attrition is when the **load** hits itself and gets smaller and rounder; abrasion is what wears away the bed and banks.
mistakes.w: Attrition is when the river erodes the bed and banks.

mistakes.r: Hydraulic action is the **force of the water** (compressed air in cracks); scraping by the load is abrasion.
mistakes.w: Hydraulic action is when rocks scrape the bed.

mistakes.r: A waterfall forms because of **differential erosion**: hard rock over soft rock, undercutting, overhang and collapse.
mistakes.w: A waterfall forms because the river drops over a cliff.

mistakes.r: Meanders form because of **faster flow and erosion on the outside bend and slower flow and deposition on the inside bend** (helicoidal flow).
mistakes.w: Meanders form because the river is trying to go round obstacles.

mistakes.r: They need **erosion** of the neck to narrow it, a flood to break through, and **deposition** to seal off the loop.
mistakes.w: Oxbow lakes are formed by deposition.

mistakes.r: Velocity generally **increases downstream** because the channel is deeper, smoother and more efficient with less friction.
mistakes.w: Rivers flow fastest in the upper course because it is steepest.

mistakes.r: The load gets **smaller and more rounded** downstream because of attrition and sorting.
Natural levees are formed by **deposition of coarse sediment** during floods; man-made ones are called embankments.
Deposition happens because the river **loses energy** (reduced velocity or discharge).
mistakes.w: Deposition happens because the river has too much energy.

summary: You must be able to describe and explain the long and cross profile of a river, the changes in the channel downstream, the processes of erosion, transportation and deposition, and how these form interlocking spurs, waterfalls and gorges, meanders, oxbow lakes, levees, floodplains and estuaries. These explanations earn the 4 and 6 mark Paper 1 marks and underpin flooding questions.

terms.d: The area of land drained by a river and its tributaries.
The boundary of high land that separates one drainage basin from another.
A cross-section of a river from its source to its mouth showing how its height changes with distance.
The shape of a river channel and valley when viewed in a slice across them.
The force of the water that compresses air in cracks in the bed and banks, weakening and removing rock.
The wearing away of the bed and banks by the river's load scraping against them.
The wearing down of the load itself as pieces knock against each other, making them smaller and rounder.
The chemical process in which soluble rock such as limestone is dissolved by water; also dissolved material carried by the river.
The transport of large boulders by rolling along the river bed.
The transport of small stones and pebbles by bouncing along the river bed.
The transport of fine silt and clay carried within the flowing water.
The volume of water passing a point in a river each second, measured in cubic metres per second (cumecs).
A deep hollow at the base of a waterfall formed by the force of the falling water and abrasion.
A narrow, steep-sided valley formed by the retreat of a waterfall.
A gentle slope of deposited sediment on the inside bend of a meander.
A natural raised bank along the side of a river channel formed by deposition of coarse sediment during floods.
The flat area of land either side of a river in its lower course that is covered with water when the river floods.
The wide, tidal mouth of a river where fresh water meets the sea.

worked.ans: A waterfall forms where a river flows over a layer of hard rock lying on top of softer rock (1). The softer rock is eroded faster by hydraulic action and abrasion, and a plunge pool is formed where the water lands and swirls rocks around (1). The hard rock is undercut and left as an overhang, which eventually collapses because it is unsupported (1). Repeated collapse makes the waterfall retreat upstream, leaving a steep-sided gorge downstream (1). (4 marks)
worked.q: Explain how a waterfall and gorge form. (4 marks)
steps: Identify hard rock over soft rock (1 mark).
Soft rock erodes faster by hydraulic action and abrasion, forming a plunge pool and undercutting (1 mark).
Overhang collapses and the waterfall retreats upstream (1 mark).
Retreat leaves a steep-sided gorge (1 mark).

worked.ans: Upper course discharge = 0.8 cumecs; downstream discharge = 19.8 cumecs. Discharge increases by 19 cumecs (about 25 times) downstream because the channel is much wider and deeper and the velocity is higher, as tributaries and groundwater add water. (4 marks)
worked.q: A river has a width of 2.5 m, an average depth of 0.4 m and a velocity of 0.8 m/s in the upper course. Downstream it is 12 m wide, 1.5 m deep with a velocity of 1.1 m/s. Calculate the discharge at each point and describe the change. (4 marks)
steps: Discharge = width x depth x velocity.

worked.ans: An oxbow lake forms from a meander in the middle or lower course of a river. Water flows fastest on the outside of each bend, so hydraulic action and abrasion erode the bank and form a river cliff, while on the inside bend the water is slow, so deposition forms a slip-off slope. Over time the outside bends migrate towards each other and the neck of land between them becomes narrower. During a flood the river has a lot of energy and breaks through the neck, taking the shortest, straightest route. Deposition then seals the ends of the old loop as the water slows at the edges of the new channel, so the meander is cut off. The cut-off loop becomes a crescent-shaped oxbow lake, which later may dry out to leave a meander scar. (6 marks)
worked.q: Explain how an oxbow lake forms. (6 marks)
steps: Start in the middle or lower course with a meander.
Erosion on outside bends narrows the neck.
Flood: river breaks through the neck and takes the shortest route.
Deposition on the edges seals off the old loop.
Lake gradually dries to a meander scar.
